items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we will discuss the negative binomial distribution, which can be thought of as an extension of the geometric distribution. It is used to model the number of independent Bernoulli trials needed to get a particular number of successes.

Content:
Let's build some intuition by considering an example.

Content:
Suppose a fair die is thrown repeatedly until a total of [MATH: \color{red}3] sixes are shown. The sixes do not need to be consecutive, so the sequence
[MATH: {\color{black}{1}},\quad
{\color{black}{4}},\quad
{\color{black}{3}},\quad
\stackrel{\color{green}{\checkmark}}{6},\quad
{\color{black}{4}},\quad
{\color{black}{3}},\quad
{\color{black}{2}},\quad
\stackrel{\color{green}{\checkmark}}{6},\quad
{\color{black}{5}},\quad
\stackrel{\color{green}{\checkmark}}{6}]
is an acceptable sequence. Note the following:

Content:
- We interpret rolling a [MATH: 6] as a "success" and anything else as "failure."
- In the above example, we have [MATH: \color{red}3] successes, [MATH: \color{blue}7] failures, and [MATH: {\color{red}{3}} + {\color{blue}{7}} = 10] throws in total.
- The sequence terminated on a success.

Content:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] model the total number of throws until we get [MATH: \color{red} 3] successes. In the example above, we have [MATH: X=10.] How do we calculate the probability that the sequence will terminate on the 10th throw?

Content:
We can calculate [MATH: P(X = 10)] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: P(X = 10) = \binom{9}{2}\left(\dfrac56\right)^{\color{blue}7}\left(\dfrac16\right)^{\color{red}3}.]

Content:
Let's break this down a little:

Content:
- The factor [MATH: \left(\dfrac16\right)^{\color{red}3}] gives the probability of getting [MATH: \color{red}3] successes.
- The factor [MATH: \left(\dfrac56\right)^{\color{blue}7}] gives the probability of getting [MATH: \color{blue}7] failures.
- The factor [MATH: \displaystyle\binom{9}{2}] is a binomial coefficient. It gives the number of ways of arranging the first [MATH: 2] successes into [MATH: 9] possible positions. We have no choice in how to arrange the third success (it has to come last), so we only consider the first two here.

Content:
The random variable [MATH: X] in this example is a negative binomial random variable. Let's now discuss negative binomial random variables more generally.

Content:
A discrete random variable [MATH: X] follows a negative binomial distribution if it has the following probability mass function:

Content:
[MATH: {((x − 1)/(r − 1))(1 − p)^{x − r}p^{r},|x = r, r + 1, r + 2, …; 0,|otherwise]

Content:
The negative binomial distribution models the number [MATH: X] of independent Bernoulli trials, each with probability [MATH: p] of success, before [MATH: r] successes occur.

Content:
It's worth taking some time to understand the above formula:

Content:
- The factor [MATH: p^{r}] gives the probability of getting [MATH: r] successes.
- The factor [MATH: (1-p)^{x-r}] gives the probability of getting [MATH: x-r] failures.
- The factor [MATH: \displaystyle\binom{x-1}{r-1}] gives the number of ways of arranging the first [MATH: r-1] successes into [MATH: x-1] positions.
- [MATH: x\geq r] because there should be a minimum of [MATH: r] Bernoulli trials before the sequence terminates.

Content:
If a random variable [MATH: X] follows a negative binomial distribution, we write

Content:
[MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(r, p).]

Content:
Finally, notice that if we set [MATH: r=1] (so the number of trials terminates after the first success), then the probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] reduces to that of a geometric distribution.

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(3, 0.8),] compute [MATH: P(X = 7),] rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(3, 0.8),] compute [MATH: P(X = 7),] rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For a negative binomial random variable [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(r, p),] we have the following probability distribution:

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(r − 1))(1 − p)^{x − r}p^{r},|x = r, r + 1, r + 2, …; 0,|otherwise]

Here, [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(3, 0.8),] so the distribution of [MATH: X] in this case is

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(2))(0.2)^{x − 3}(0.8)^{3},|x = 3, 4, 5, …; 0,|otherwise.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X = 7)|= f(7); = ((7 − 1)/(2))(0.2)^{7 − 3}(0.8)^{3}; = ((6)/(2))(0.2)^{4}(0.8)^{3}; ≈ 0.0123]

rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: Given [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(6, 0.28),] compute [MATH: P(X < 9),] rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.
sections.readable_text: Given [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(6, 0.28),] compute [MATH: P(X < 9),] rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For a negative binomial random variable [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(r, p),] we have the following probability distribution:

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(r − 1))(1 − p)^{x − r}p^{r},|x = r, r + 1, r + 2, …; 0,|otherwise]

Here, [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(6, 0.28),] so the distribution of [MATH: X] in this case is

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(5))(0.72)^{x − 6}(0.28)^{6},|x = 6, 7, 8, …; 0,|otherwise.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X < 9)|= P(X ∈ {6, 7, 8}); = P(X = 6) + P(X = 7) + P(X = 8); = f(6) + f(7) + f(8); = ((5)/(5))(0.72)^{0}(0.28)^{6} + ((6)/(5))(0.72)^{1}(0.28)^{6} + ((7)/(5))(0.72)^{2}(0.28)^{6}; ≈ 0.0078]

rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

sections.readable_text: Given [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(11, 0.6),] compute [MATH: P(12< X < 16),] rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:

Here, [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(11, 0.6),] so the distribution of [MATH: X] in this case is

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(10))(0.4)^{x − 11}(0.6)^{11},|x = 11, 12, 13, …; 0,|otherwise.]

[MATH: P(12 < X < 16)|= P(X ∈ {13, 14, 15}); = P(X = 13) + P(X = 14) + P(X = 15); = f(13) + f(14) + f(15); = ((12)/(10))(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{11} + ((13)/(10))(0.4)^{3}(0.6)^{11} + ((14)/(10))(0.4)^{4}(0.6)^{11}; ≈ 0.1977]

rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html:
For a negative binomial random variable [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(r, p),] we have the following probability distribution:

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(r − 1))(1 − p)^{x − r}p^{r},|x = r, r + 1, r + 2, …; 0,|otherwise]

Here, [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(14,0.65),] so the distribution of [MATH: X] in this case is

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(13))(0.35)^{x − 14}(0.65)^{14},|x = 14, 15, 16, …; 0,|otherwise.]

There are infinitely many values of [MATH: X] such that [MATH: X \geq 16.] However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

[MATH: P(X ≥ 16)|= 1 − P(X < 16)]

Computing the complement, we get

[MATH: P(X < 16)|= P(X ∈ {14, 15}); = P(X = 14) + P(X = 15); = f(14) + f(15); = ((13)/(13))(0.35)^{0}(0.65)^{14} + ((14)/(13))(0.35)^{1}(0.65)^{14}; ≈ 0.0142.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X ≥ 16)|= 1 − P(X < 16); ≈ 1 − 0.0142; = 0.9858]

rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will discuss the negative binomial distribution, which can be thought of as an extension of the geometric distribution. It is used to model the number of independent Bernoulli trials needed to get a particular number of successes.

Content:
Let's build some intuition by considering an example.

Content:
Suppose a fair die is thrown repeatedly until a total of [MATH: \color{red}3] sixes are shown. The sixes do not need to be consecutive, so the sequence
[MATH: {\color{black}{1}},\quad
{\color{black}{4}},\quad
{\color{black}{3}},\quad
\stackrel{\color{green}{\checkmark}}{6},\quad
{\color{black}{4}},\quad
{\color{black}{3}},\quad
{\color{black}{2}},\quad
\stackrel{\color{green}{\checkmark}}{6},\quad
{\color{black}{5}},\quad
\stackrel{\color{green}{\checkmark}}{6}]
is an acceptable sequence. Note the following:

Content:
- We interpret rolling a [MATH: 6] as a "success" and anything else as "failure."
- In the above example, we have [MATH: \color{red}3] successes, [MATH: \color{blue}7] failures, and [MATH: {\color{red}{3}} + {\color{blue}{7}} = 10] throws in total.
- The sequence terminated on a success.

Content:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] model the total number of throws until we get [MATH: \color{red} 3] successes. In the example above, we have [MATH: X=10.] How do we calculate the probability that the sequence will terminate on the 10th throw?

Content:
We can calculate [MATH: P(X = 10)] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: P(X = 10) = \binom{9}{2}\left(\dfrac56\right)^{\color{blue}7}\left(\dfrac16\right)^{\color{red}3}.]

Content:
Let's break this down a little:

Content:
- The factor [MATH: \left(\dfrac16\right)^{\color{red}3}] gives the probability of getting [MATH: \color{red}3] successes.
- The factor [MATH: \left(\dfrac56\right)^{\color{blue}7}] gives the probability of getting [MATH: \color{blue}7] failures.
- The factor [MATH: \displaystyle\binom{9}{2}] is a binomial coefficient. It gives the number of ways of arranging the first [MATH: 2] successes into [MATH: 9] possible positions. We have no choice in how to arrange the third success (it has to come last), so we only consider the first two here.

Content:
The random variable [MATH: X] in this example is a negative binomial random variable. Let's now discuss negative binomial random variables more generally.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Probability Mass Function of a Negative Binomial Random Variable

Content:
A discrete random variable [MATH: X] follows a negative binomial distribution if it has the following probability mass function:

Content:
[MATH: {((x − 1)/(r − 1))(1 − p)^{x − r}p^{r},|x = r, r + 1, r + 2, …; 0,|otherwise]

Content:
The negative binomial distribution models the number [MATH: X] of independent Bernoulli trials, each with probability [MATH: p] of success, before [MATH: r] successes occur.

Content:
It's worth taking some time to understand the above formula:

Content:
- The factor [MATH: p^{r}] gives the probability of getting [MATH: r] successes.
- The factor [MATH: (1-p)^{x-r}] gives the probability of getting [MATH: x-r] failures.
- The factor [MATH: \displaystyle\binom{x-1}{r-1}] gives the number of ways of arranging the first [MATH: r-1] successes into [MATH: x-1] positions.
- [MATH: x\geq r] because there should be a minimum of [MATH: r] Bernoulli trials before the sequence terminates.

Content:
If a random variable [MATH: X] follows a negative binomial distribution, we write

Content:
[MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(r, p).]

Content:
Finally, notice that if we set [MATH: r=1] (so the number of trials terminates after the first success), then the probability mass function [MATH: f(x)] reduces to that of a geometric distribution.

---

Item 3 — Example: Computing a Probability at a Point

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(3, 0.8),] compute [MATH: P(X = 7),] rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For a negative binomial random variable [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(r, p),] we have the following probability distribution:

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(r − 1))(1 − p)^{x − r}p^{r},|x = r, r + 1, r + 2, …; 0,|otherwise]

Here, [MATH: X \sim \textrm{NB}(3, 0.8),] so the distribution of [MATH: X] in this case is

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(2))(0.2)^{x − 3}(0.8)^{3},|x = 3, 4, 5, …; 0,|otherwise.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X = 7)|= f(7); = ((7 − 1)/(2))(0.2)^{7 − 3}(0.8)^{3}; = ((6)/(2))(0.2)^{4}(0.8)^{3}; ≈ 0.0123]

rounded to [MATH: 4] decimal places.

[MATH: {((x − 1)/(5))(0.72)^{x − 6}(0.28)^{6},|x = 6, 7, 8, …; 0,|otherwise.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X < 9)|= P(X ∈ {6, 7, 8}); = P(X = 6) + P(X = 7) + P(X = 8); = f(6) + f(7) + f(8); = ((5)/(5))(0.72)^{0}(0.28)^{6} + ((6)/(5))(0.72)^{1}(0.28)^{6} + ((7)/(5))(0.72)^{2}(0.28)^{6}; ≈ 0.0078]
